# Async::DBD::Pg

Event-loop agnostic async PostgreSQL client for Perl. Built on DBI/DBD::Pg
with Future::IO, so it runs under any Future::IO implementation (UV,
IO::Async, GLib). Every method below that says `await` returns a Future.

Requires Perl 5.24+, DBD::Pg 3.20.0+.

## Getting started

    use Future::AsyncAwait;
    use Future::IO;
    use Async::DBD::Pg;

    # Required: without it Future::IO drives one filehandle at a time and
    # the pool runs serially, with no error and no warning.
    BEGIN { Future::IO->load_best_impl }

    my $pg = Async::DBD::Pg->new(dsn => 'postgresql://user:pass@host/db');

    # await is legal only inside an async sub.
    (async sub {
        my $row   = await $pg->query_row('SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = $1', 42);
        my $count = await $pg->query_value('SELECT count(*) FROM users');
        my $rs    = await $pg->query('SELECT id, name FROM users');
    })->()->get;

    await $pg->shutdown(timeout => 5);

## Placeholders

Two forms, not mixable in one statement:

    await $pg->query('SELECT * FROM t WHERE id = $1 AND x = $2', 1, 'a');
    await $pg->query('SELECT * FROM t WHERE id = :id', { id => 1 });

`?` is NOT a placeholder here, so PostgreSQL's own operators work unescaped:

    await $pg->query(q{SELECT data ? 'key' FROM docs});      # jsonb exists
    await $pg->query('SELECT tags[:2] FROM posts');           # array slice

Binary and other typed values must say their type, or a NUL byte silently
truncates the value. The type may be a constant or a name:

    use DBD::Pg qw(:pg_types);
    await $pg->query('INSERT INTO f (body) VALUES ($1)',
        { type => PG_BYTEA, value => $bytes });
    await $pg->query('INSERT INTO f (body) VALUES ($1)',
        { type => 'bytea', value => $bytes });

Names are DBD::Pg's PG_* constants lowercased ('bytea', 'jsonb'), resolved
from a load-time map, so no round trip. A type DBD::Pg does not know (a user
enum, an extension type) croaks -- it cannot be bound by type at all, so bind
it untyped or cast in SQL. Note 'char' is PG_CHAR (1 byte); SQL CHAR(n) is
'bpchar'.

## Pool: Async::DBD::Pg

    Async::DBD::Pg->new(dsn => $dsn, min_connections => 2, max_connections => 10);
    await $pg->query($sql, @bind);        # Results
    await $pg->query_row($sql, @bind);    # one hashref, or undef
    await $pg->query_value($sql, @bind);  # one value, or undef
    await $pg->query_list($sql, @bind);   # one row as a list: my ($id, $name) = ...
    await $pg->connection;                # check out a Connection yourself
    await $pg->with_connection($code, @args);  # scoped checkout, always released
    await $pg->transaction($code, @args);      # commit, or rollback and rethrow
    await $pg->shutdown(timeout => 5);
    $pg->on_query(sub { my ($e) = @_ });  # {sql, binds, elapsed, rows, error, cached, connection}
    $pg->server_version;                  # 160014, integer, for feature gating
    $pg->stats;  $pg->idle_count;  $pg->active_count;  $pg->waiting_count;
    $pg->total_count;  $pg->is_healthy;  $pg->is_shut_down;  $pg->safe_dsn;

Constructor options: `dsn`, `min_connections`, `max_connections`,
`connect_timeout`, `statement_timeout`, `max_queries`, `statement_cache_size`,
`on_connect`, `on_release`, `on_log`, `on_query`, `reconnect`.

`statement_cache_size` defaults to 0 (off) and caches only statements carrying
placeholders. It saves planning, not round trips: no measurable gain on
trivially planned statements, ~22% on a join-heavy workload over loopback. A
cache too small for the working set thrashes and is slower than leaving it off.

`with_connection` and `transaction` take `async sub { my ($conn, @args) = @_ }`
and forward trailing arguments, so values can be passed rather than closed
over. A transaction holds its connection across every await inside the body.

## Connection: Async::DBD::Pg::Connection

    await $conn->query($sql, @bind);
    await $conn->query($sql, @bind, { timeout => 5 });
    await $conn->query_row($sql, @bind);
    await $conn->query_value($sql, @bind);
    await $conn->transaction($code, @args);   # nests via savepoints
    await $conn->transaction({ retry => 3 }, $code);  # retries 40001/40P01 only
    await $conn->advisory_lock($key);         # xact-scoped; inside a transaction
    await $conn->try_advisory_lock($key);     # false rather than waiting
    await $conn->cursor($sql, @bind, { batch_size => 100 });
    $conn->cancel;  $conn->release;  $conn->dbh;
    $conn->in_transaction;  $conn->is_released;  $conn->query_count;
    $conn->id;  $conn->server_version;

## Results: Async::DBD::Pg::Results

Rows are stored positionally; hashes are derived on demand.

    $r->rows          # Collection of hashrefs   (croaks if names repeat)
    $r->arrays        # Collection of arrayrefs  (always works)
    $r->columns       # ['id', 'name']
    $r->types         # ['int4', 'text']
    $r->count  $r->rows_affected  $r->is_empty  $r->elapsed

    $r->first         # first row, or undef  (croaks if names repeat)
    $r->single        # first row, warns if more than one matched
    $r->first_value   # first column of first row, no complaint
    $r->single_value  # same, but warns if more than one row matched
    $r->first_list    # my ($id, $name) = $r->first_list  (arrayref in scalar ctx)
    $r->single_list   # same, but warns if more than one row matched
    $r->row_array($i) # one row, positional
    $r->next  $r->reset  $r->all
    $r->get_column($name_or_index)   # a Column
    $r->preview       # short typed table for logs and debugging
    $r->map_rows(sub { my ($row, $names) = @_; ... })  # Collection, positional

Views (new object, shared rows, own iterator position):

    $r->as(['a_id', 'b_id'])         # rename all, by position
    $r->as({ 0 => 'a_id' })          # rename some, by index
    $r->multi                        # Hash::MultiValue rows, lossless
    $r->expand                       # decode json/jsonb columns
    $r->by('id')                     # { 42 => $row }, croaks if keys repeat
    $r->groups('dept')               # { eng => Collection }, lossless

### Repeated column names

`SELECT *` across a join can return two columns named `id`. A hash cannot
hold both, so every method that builds a hashref croaks rather than silently
dropping a value:

    Column 'id' appears 2 times at positions 0, 1;
    alias the columns in your SQL, or use ->arrays or ->as

Positional access still works on that result: `arrays`, `row_array`,
`columns`, `types`, `single_value`, `preview`, `get_column` by index. So does
`multi`, which is lossless. The usual fix is to alias in SQL, or `->as`.

## Collection: Async::DBD::Pg::Collection

A blessed arrayref, so `@$collection`, `$collection->[0]`, `map`, `grep`,
`sort` all work.

    $collection->size  $collection->first  $collection->last
    $collection->each($cb, @args)
    $collection->compact    # drops undef only, not '' or 0
    $collection->join($sep)  $collection->to_array

No `map`/`grep`/`sort`/`reduce` methods: the builtins are shorter and it is
already an arrayref.

## Column: Async::DBD::Pg::Column

    $col->name  $col->index
    $col->all         # Collection of values
    $col->first  $col->next  $col->reset

`next` yields values, so a NULL, `''` or `0` ends a `while (my $v = ...)`
loop early. Test with `defined`, or use `all`.

## Cursor: Async::DBD::Pg::Cursor

Streams a large result without holding it in memory.

    my $cur = await $conn->cursor('SELECT * FROM big', { batch_size => 500 });
    while (my $row = await $cur->next) { ... }   # one row at a time
    await $cur->each(sub { my ($row) = @_ }, @args);
    await $cur->all;                             # Collection of rows
    await $cur->close;
    $cur->name;  $cur->batch_size;  $cur->is_exhausted;  $cur->is_closed;

`batch_size` is rows per round trip, not what `next` returns. No `reset`: a
server-side cursor is consumed, and re-running the query is a different
guarantee.

## Pub/sub: Async::DBD::Pg::PubSub

LISTEN/NOTIFY on a dedicated connection. Channels are a per-database
broadcast namespace, not a work queue.

    await $pg->listen('channel', sub { my ($payload, $channel) = @_ });
    await $pg->notify('channel', $payload);
    await $pg->unlisten('channel');
    await $pg->unlisten_all;
    my $ps = $pg->pubsub;
    $ps->is_connected;  $ps->subscribed_channels;

## Errors

Failures are objects that stringify, thrown as exceptions:

    Async::DBD::Pg::Error::Query          # ->state, ->state_name, ->constraint,
                                          # ->detail, ->hint, ->table, ->column,
                                          # ->is_retryable, ->is_unique_violation,
                                          # ->is_foreign_key_violation,
                                          # ->is_not_null_violation
    Async::DBD::Pg::Error::Connection
    Async::DBD::Pg::Error::PoolExhausted
    Async::DBD::Pg::Error::Timeout

## Gotchas

- `Results` is stateful: `next` advances a shared position; call `reset`.
- `count` is rows in hand; `rows_affected` is what an INSERT/UPDATE changed.
- `arrays` and `row_array` hand back the result's own arrayrefs, not copies;
  writing through one changes what `rows` and every view report.
- `get_column` reads an all-digit argument as an index, so a column aliased
  `AS "2"` is unreachable by name there.
- `Column::next` yields values, so NULL, `''` or `0` ends a `while` loop
  early; test with `defined`.
